title: Celebrating Jerusalem's Finished Wall
overview: After lists of priests and temple workers across several generations, Jerusalem holds a joyful ceremony to dedicate its rebuilt wall to God and sets up steady support for those who serve at the temple.

parts.label: Priests of the first return (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: These are the leading priests and Levites (temple assistants) who came home from exile in Babylon nearly a century earlier with Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. The Jeremiah and Ezra named here are probably not the famous prophet and scribe, and Mattaniah led the thanksgiving songs, with singers grouped to face and answer each other.

parts.label: The high priests' family line (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: This traces the high priests from Joshua down to Jaddua, father to son. The chapter does not say why it is included, though many interpreters think that with no king on the throne, such a list helped mark time and confirm each priest's ancestry.

parts.label: The next generation and records (vv. 12-26)
parts.note: Sons now lead the same priestly families their fathers had, and these names were kept in official records. The Levites sang in two answering groups, following a pattern credited to King David, while gatekeepers guarded the storerooms.

parts.label: Gathering and purifying (vv. 27-30)
parts.note: Levites and musicians were called in from the villages around Jerusalem for the celebration. The priests made themselves ritually clean, then the people, gates and wall, setting them apart for God, though the text does not say exactly how this was done.

parts.label: Two choirs on the wall (vv. 31-43)
parts.note: Two large choirs walked in opposite directions along the top of the wall, Ezra leading one and Nehemiah following the other, and met at the temple. There they offered many sacrifices, and everyone, women and children included, rejoiced so loudly the sound carried far away.

parts.label: Supporting temple workers (vv. 44-47)
parts.note: People were put in charge of storerooms for the gifts the Law required, such as the first part of the harvest and a tenth of produce, to provide for the priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers. The Levites in turn set aside a share of what they received for the priests, the descendants of Aaron.

think: When something long and hard is finally finished, what makes marking it together with others feel meaningful rather than just noise?
